Need to search first.I could only collect part of what you asked for. The research tool hit its usage limit after one search, so I couldn't open any full pages. Everything below comes from the passages of four commentaries that this one search returned: David Guzik (Enduring Word), Matthew Henry (Blue Letter Bible), the Pulpit Commentary (BibleHub), and two short Enduring Word devotionals. Because I only saw passages, some verses have no notes. **I found nothing at all for parts 2 and 3:** no differences between Protestant traditions, no modern scholarship, no Catholic or Orthodox readings, and no prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. The Precept Austin passage I got only covered the later part of the chapter (vv. 35–48), so it isn't used.

**Source URLs**

- [MH] https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_012.cfm
- [PC] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/12.htm

---

**v. 1 (with vv. 1–3):**
- Guzik says hypocrisy works like leaven: a small amount spreads and sours everything. Jesus gives this warning especially for times when disciples are popular and doing well outwardly. [EW]
- Henry says the disciples were going to preach to others. If they twisted the message or acted deceitfully, hypocrisy would be worse in them than in other people. [MH]

**vv. 2–3:** Nothing specific found beyond the note on vv. 1–3.

**v. 4:**
- The Pulpit Commentary sees "My friends" as a tender term. Jesus uses it for the disciples near Him while telling them about the hard life ahead. [PC, in its comments on v. 32]
- Guzik connects the verse to the rising opposition in Luke 11:53–54. The disciples were probably feeling anxious as the crucifixion drew closer and needed to get fear into perspective. [EW]

**vv. 4–5:**
- Guzik says persecutors can kill and do nothing more, while God has final power over the believer's life and death. The right response is a healthy respect for God that cares more about obeying Him than any person. [EW]
- Henry points to Moses, who overcame his fear of the king's anger by looking to the God who is invisible. Owning Christ may bring human anger, but that can go no further than death, and only with God's permission. Denying Christ brings God's anger, which can send a person to hell, and no one can resist it. [MH]
- The Pulpit Commentary says suffering and even death cannot happen to Christ's servants without God's consent. Knowing this should give them courage, along with the warm welcome from God that awaits anyone who dies this way. [PC]

**vv. 6–7:**
- Guzik's chapter summary says both greed and worry come from not truly understanding how much God values us and cares for us. [EW]

**v. 10:**
- The Pulpit Commentary says forgiveness for speaking against the Son of Man reaches even people who deny Him out of fear of others or love of the world, though they knew He was their Redeemer. It calls this one of the most hopeful passages in the New Testament about sin that will finally be forgiven. [PC]
- It also says the verse does not teach universal salvation, because the very next sentence names a sin that will never be forgiven. [PC]
- It defines blasphemy against the Holy Spirit in this context as the settled hatred of holiness that led the Pharisee leaders to credit Jesus' good works to the spirit of evil. [PC]

**vv. 11–12:**
- Guzik sees this promise fulfilled in Acts 4, when the Spirit gave Peter and John the right words before the authorities. [EW-11]
- Their message was not something they made up. It was what they had seen and heard about Jesus, passed on as eyewitnesses. [EW-11]

**v. 13:**
- Guzik says that under the law of the time the elder brother got two-thirds and the younger one-third. [EW-13]
- He notes that the man didn't ask Jesus to hear both sides. He asked Jesus to take his side against his brother. [EW-13]
- Henry suggests the brother may really have wronged him by grabbing the whole estate. Anyone wronged like this can take the matter to God, who brings justice for the oppressed. [MH]

**v. 14:**
- Guzik says Jesus didn't see it as His job to settle every dispute. A person can fight for what is rightly theirs and end up worse off than if they had let it go and left it with God. [EW]
- He also warns against using a false concern for justice to cover a selfish agenda. [EW-13]
- Henry draws lessons about Christ's kingdom. It is spiritual, not of this world. It does not interfere with civil government or civil rights. It does not promise worldly advantages to disciples. It encourages giving up one's rights for the sake of peace rather than pressing hard demands. [MH]

**v. 15:**
- Guzik cites Morris: the Greek word means "guard yourselves," because everyone is under attack from greed. [EW]
- He suggests the man's request may have been driven more by greed than by a desire for justice. [EW]
- He says living as if life consists in possessions is greed, and greed is idolatry (Colossians 3:5). [EW]
- He also quotes Clarke, who links great wealth with pride, idleness and luxury, and Morgan: dividing property between greedy men only sets up the next fight. [EW]
- The Pulpit Commentary says Jesus saw greed behind the question, not anger at a real wrong. "Life" here can fairly be read as a person's true life. Jesus' own life, with no land, home or money, illustrated the point, yet people in every age have refused to accept His view. [PC]

**vv. 16–19:**
- Guzik says the parable does not condemn wealth itself. It condemns a man who lived with no thought of eternity, never gave his possessions over to God, and had no treasure in heaven. [EW]
- Henry describes it as the story of a rich man cut off suddenly by death in the middle of his worldly plans. [MH]

**vv. 20–21:**
- Guzik says everyone would have called the man a success, but God called him a fool. Putting things first is not only sin but also stupid. [EW]
- On "Whose will those things be?": they did not belong to God, because the man never gave them to God, and they did not belong to him, because he couldn't take them with him. Guzik suggests they may in a sense have belonged to the devil. [EW]

**vv. 22–23:**
- Guzik says greed and worry are closely linked. Greed never thinks it has enough; worry fears it will never have enough. Neither keeps its eyes on Jesus. [EW]
- He adds that worry brings a person down to the level of an animal focused only on physical needs, when life is meant for eternal things. [EW]
- Henry argues that God gave us life and a body without any planning on our part. That is the greater gift, so we can trust Him for the lesser things, food and clothing. [MH]

**v. 24:**
- Guzik says much worry comes from a low view of our own worth to God. [EW]
- Henry says the God who feeds lesser creatures can be trusted to provide for His people. [MH]

**vv. 25–28:** Guzik groups these as "reasons not to worry," but the passage I saw had no detailed notes on them. [EW]

**vv. 29–30:**
- Guzik says believers don't have to cling to this world's things. Jesus gave up everything heaven held and was content to simply trust God. [EW]
- He reads "the nations of the world seek" as a contrast between people who don't know God and people who know Him and receive His care. [EW]
- He adds that Jesus didn't only say to stop worrying but to replace worry with a concern for God's kingdom (leading into v. 31). [EW]
